title: Tourism
intro: Seven driver–tourist scenarios rewritten for young professionals aiming at hotel front office, guest relations and other customer-facing roles. Each has 20 lines or fewer, alternating between the local speaker and the tourist, with a setting, cast, resolution and coaching notes ending in a “say this, not that” fix. The full set of 20 is on the tourism role-play Page.

scenarios.title: Finding a landmark address: a passer-by helps
scenarios.setting: Galle Road, Kollupitiya, Colombo, mid-afternoon. A tourist with a backpack is standing at a bus stop, looking at her phone.
scenarios.characters: Passer-by: Nimali, 26, a bank officer walking back to her office after lunch. Tourist: Emma, 24, a backpacker from the UK with a guesthouse address on her phone.
scenarios.resolution: Emma finds the right lane: the passer-by explains the sub-number, gives step-by-step directions to the landmark, checks that Emma understood, and adds a tip for the evening.

notes.text: Open with an offer, not a question about where they're from: “You look a little lost. Can I help?” is friendly without being pushy.
Ask for the landmark early: “Did your host mention a landmark?” is the most useful question for any Sri Lankan address.
Give directions in order, one landmark per step (straight, past the bank, second left, then what they'll see), and let the tourist repeat them back.

sayThis.say: “The pharmacy is opposite the Bo tree”, not “The pharmacy is in front of the Bo tree.” In international English, “in front of” means on the same side, facing it.

lines.text: Excuse me, you look a little lost. Can I help you find something?
Oh, yes please! I'm looking for my guesthouse: 27/3 Temple Lane, Kollupitiya. My map says it's here, but it isn't.
May I see the address? Temple Lane is close. Did your host mention a landmark? A few lanes here have similar names.
He said it's near a big Bo tree and a pharmacy. What's a Bo tree?
It's a sacred fig tree, usually with a small shrine and prayer flags around it. The one on Temple Lane is easy to spot.
Great. And what does 27/3 mean? Is it flat three?
Not exactly. 27 is the main number on the road, and the 3 means the third house in a small lane beside number 27.
Ah, a sub-address. That explains why my map pin is in the wrong place.
Yes, map pins here are often a little off. Go straight along Galle Road, past the bank, and take the second turn on the left.
Second left after the bank. How far is it?
About five minutes' walk. You'll see the Bo tree on your right, and the pharmacy is opposite it.
Opposite, so across the road from the tree?
Exactly. If you can't find the gate, call your host from outside the pharmacy. He'll come out to meet you.
That's really helpful. Is there anywhere nice to go this evening?
Galle Face Green is a lovely walk at sunset, about ten minutes from here by tuk-tuk. Try the isso vadai, the prawn fritters from the stalls.
Galle Face at sunset. I'll go tonight!
Just take care crossing Galle Road. The traffic is fast, so use the pedestrian crossing near the bank.
I will. Thank you so much, you've saved my afternoon.
You're welcome. Enjoy Colombo!

scenarios.title: Is that fare fair? Booking a PickMe at the front desk
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a city hotel in Kandy, early evening.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Ruwani, 27, front office executive. Tourist: Lukas Weber, 31, from Germany, staying three nights, who has just been quoted a tuk-tuk fare outside.
scenarios.resolution: Lukas learns what a fair fare looks like, gets a PickMe booked by the front desk at the app price, keeps cash for the driver, and has the hotel's number to book his ride back.

notes.text: Greet the guest by name and offer help first: “How may I help you?”
When a guest asks if a price is fair, give a range and the reason (distance, traffic) without criticising drivers: “It's your choice. Many drivers here are honest.”
Offer to do the task for the guest, then give the details they need: the wait time, the driver's name and the number plate. Mention “cash only” before the ride.

sayThis.say: “I'll book a PickMe for you now”, not “I'll put a PickMe for you.” And “Please ask the driver to use the meter”, not “Tell him to put the meter.”

lines.text: Good evening, Mr. Weber. How may I help you?
Hi. I'd like to go to a restaurant on Ampitiya Road tonight. A tuk-tuk driver outside offered 1,200 rupees. Is that fair?
It's about four kilometres, so that's a little high. On the PickMe app, it's usually around 700 to 900 rupees, depending on traffic.
So should I say no to him?
It's your choice, sir. Many drivers here are honest. If you take a street tuk-tuk, ask for the meter, or agree the price before you get in.
How do I know the meter is working?
It should show zero when you set off, and you can watch the fare as you go. If there's no meter, agree the price first.
Okay. Or could you book an app ride for me? I don't have PickMe.
Certainly. I'll book a PickMe tuk-tuk for you now. The fare is shown before the ride, and you pay the driver at the end.
Can I pay by card?
Most tuk-tuks take cash only, so please keep some small notes. If you need rupees, there's an ATM in our lobby.
I have cash, thanks. How long will it take?
The app says six minutes. Your driver is Sampath, in a blue tuk-tuk, and I've written the number plate on this slip.
Great. And how do I get back after dinner?
The restaurant can call a tuk-tuk for you, or call us on this number and we'll book one. Here's our card.
Perfect. That's very helpful.
My pleasure. Your driver is at the main entrance now. Enjoy your dinner, Mr. Weber.

scenarios.title: Arranging a day hire at the front desk, and the head wobble
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a boutique hotel inside Galle Fort, the evening before a day trip.
scenarios.characters: Front office manager: Sanjaya, 34, front office manager who arranges tours with the hotel's approved drivers. Tourist: Sophie Clarke, 38, from Australia, travelling with her partner.
scenarios.resolution: Sophie gets the hotel's approved driver for 13,000 rupees with fuel and parking included, knows the extra-hour rate, charges it to her room, and receives the details by email.

notes.text: Give the price with what it includes in the same sentence; when the guest compares, ask what the other quote includes rather than criticising it.
Take the guest's counter-offer to the supplier yourself and report back clearly. The guest should never feel they have to bargain with the hotel.
The head wobble confuses many visitors. Always say the word as well: “He's happy with 13,000.” Then confirm everything in writing (price, stops, finish time, extra-hour rate).

sayThis.say: “The price includes fuel”, not “Fuel also included in the price.”

lines.text: Good evening, Ms. Clarke. I understand you'd like a car and driver for tomorrow. How can I help?
Yes. We'd like to see Unawatuna, a tea plantation and Mirissa, then come back to Galle. What would that cost?
Our approved driver charges 15,000 rupees for the day, for about 120 kilometres. That includes the car, the driver, fuel and parking.
That's more than I expected. A driver on the street said 12,000.
I understand. It's worth checking whether his price includes the tea factory and the waiting time. Ours includes both.
That's fair. Could you ask if he'd do 13,000?
Of course. Let me call him now. (Speaks on the phone, then smiles and gives a quick sideways head wobble.)
Sorry, was that a yes or a no? I can't tell.
Sorry, Ms. Clarke! That head movement means yes. He's happy with 13,000, if you're back by six.
Ha, thanks for explaining. Does the car have air-conditioning?
Yes, it does. Entry tickets and lunch are separate, so there are no surprises.
Good. Do we pay now?
You can pay the driver in cash at the end of the day, or we can add it to your room bill, whichever you prefer.
The room bill is easier. What time do we start?
Eight o'clock is best, before it gets hot. Your driver, Saman, will meet you here in the lobby at 7:55.
And if we want to stay longer in Mirissa?
After six, it's 1,000 rupees an hour, and he'll always ask you first. I'll email you all the details tonight.
Sounds perfect. Thank you.
You're welcome. Have a lovely evening, and enjoy your day out tomorrow.

scenarios.title: How does tipping work? A question at checkout
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a beach hotel in Bentota at checkout, the last morning of a seven-day trip.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Pradeep, 29, front office officer. Tourist: Mark Thompson, 55, from Canada, unsure what to tip.
scenarios.resolution: Mark learns to check bills for the service charge, knows how to tip his driver and guides, leaves a tip for the hotel team through the staff box, and is sent the review link.

notes.text: Answer tipping questions honestly and without pressure; never hint at a tip for yourself.
Point out the service charge on bills, including your own hotel's. Guests are grateful not to pay twice.
Close a checkout with three things: the review request, the next step (the car to the airport) and a warm goodbye.

sayThis.say: “A tip isn't expected, but it's appreciated”, not “Tip is your wish.” When you receive one: “That's very kind of you”, not “No need, no need.”

lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Are you checking out today? I hope you enjoyed your stay.
Very much, thank you. Can I ask you something a bit awkward? How does tipping work here?
It's not awkward at all. A tip isn't expected, but it's always appreciated.
I've been tipping everywhere. Was that right?
Many hotels and restaurants, including ours, add a 10% service charge to the bill. If you see it, you don't need to add more.
Oh, I didn't check. I added 10% on top a few times.
That was very generous! In small places with no service charge, rounding up is fine.
And for our driver and the guides? I'd like to get it right.
Many guests give a little for each day, but it's really your choice. Some give more if the trip went very well.
Is cash better?
Cash in rupees is easiest. Dollars or euros are fine too, but notes only, because coins can't be changed.
Ah, I have some euro coins. I'll keep those. Can I leave something for the housekeeping team?
Thank you, that's very kind. You can use the staff tip box here at the desk, and it's shared among the whole team.
Here you are. Is there somewhere I can leave a review?
That would mean a lot to us. I'll email you the link with your bill.
Will do. Anything I should know for the airport?
Your car is booked for ten o'clock. Allow about two hours to the airport, and keep your passport and ticket handy.
Thanks for everything.
It was our pleasure, Mr. Thompson. Have a safe flight, and we hope to welcome you back soon.

scenarios.title: Safety tips before a Yala safari: the concierge briefing
scenarios.setting: Hotel lobby in Tissamaharama, near Yala National Park, 4:50 a.m., while the guests wait for their safari jeep.
scenarios.characters: Concierge: Kasun, 30, guest relations and concierge officer who books the hotel's safaris. Tourist: Julien Martin, 33, from France, on safari with a friend.
scenarios.resolution: Julien knows the rules before he leaves the hotel: stay in the jeep, keep a safe distance, no feeding, keep quiet, and what to do if an elephant approaches.

notes.text: Ask permission before a briefing (“May I give you a few safety tips?”), then keep a short list in your head: jeep, distance, food, noise, elephants.
Explain the reason (“it stresses the animals”) and give the guest a voice (“please tell your driver”), so they support the rules.
Add a small extra (a breakfast box, binoculars) and close with the next step: “Your jeep has just arrived.”

sayThis.say: “Please don't get out of the jeep”, not “Please don't get down from the jeep.”

lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Martin. Your safari jeep will be here at five. May I give you a few safety tips before you go?
Of course.
Inside the park, please stay in the jeep, except at the safe rest areas. Elephants and leopards can come very close.
Understood. Can we stand up to take photos?
You can stand when the jeep stops, but please sit down when it moves. The tracks are bumpy.
What if we see a leopard? Can we ask the driver to get closer?
Your driver and the park tracker will stop at a safe distance. If many jeeps are there, they wait their turn. They don't chase animals or block their path.
Good to hear. I've read about jeeps crowding leopards.
It happens, and it stresses the animals. If you feel you're too close, please tell your driver. A good safari is quiet and patient.
Should we bring snacks?
We've packed a breakfast box for you. Please eat it at the rest area, don't feed any animals, not even the monkeys, and keep all plastic in the jeep.
And noise? My friend likes to talk.
Talking softly is fine, but no shouting or music, please. You'll see more animals that way.
Ha, I'll tell him. What if an elephant walks towards us?
Stay calm and quiet, and follow the driver's lead. He'll keep the engine running and move back slowly. Never shout or wave at an elephant.
Okay. How long is the safari?
About four hours, so you'll be back before it gets too hot. There's water in the jeep, and here's a pair of binoculars for you.
That's very thoughtful. Thank you.
My pleasure. Your jeep has just arrived. Enjoy Yala, and watch the trees: leopards like to rest on the branches.

scenarios.title: SIM cards, cash and cards on the first morning
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a hotel in Colombo, the morning after a late-night arrival.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Anusha, 25, front office officer. Tourist: Kenji Tanaka, 30, from Japan, on his first trip to South Asia, who arrived too late to buy a SIM at the airport.
scenarios.resolution: Kenji knows where to buy and register a SIM, takes rupees from the lobby ATM in local currency, and has clear rules on where cards and cash work and how to keep his card safe.

notes.text: Greet by name and link to what you know (“after your late arrival”); it shows you read the booking.
Don't quote prices that change; send the guest to the official price board. Explain the “pay in your own currency?” ATM question simply: choose rupees.
Offer a bridge until the problem is solved (the Wi-Fi password) and close with an open offer of more help.

sayThis.say: “There's an ATM here in the lobby”, not “ATM is there in the lobby.”

lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Tanaka, and welcome to Colombo. I hope you slept well after your late arrival.
Yes, thank you. I need a SIM card and some cash today. Where can I get them?
There's a Dialog shop two minutes' walk from the hotel, and we have an ATM here in the lobby. Shall I show you on the map?
Yes, please. Which SIM is best?
Dialog and Mobitel have good coverage almost everywhere, and Hutch is fine in the cities. You'll need your passport to register.
Passport, okay. How much is it?
The shop shows its tourist packages on a board, with data and prices, so you can compare.
Good. Can I pay by card there?
Usually, yes. But many small shops, tuk-tuks and buses take cash only, so please carry some rupees.
How much cash should I take?
Enough for a few days of small things. Hotels and bigger restaurants take cards, and you can charge meals here to your room.
I'll try the lobby ATM now. Oh, it's asking if I want to pay in yen or in rupees.
Please choose rupees. If you choose yen, the machine sets the exchange rate, and it's usually worse.
Rupees. Okay, done. Is it safe to use ATMs in town?
Yes, but use ATMs inside banks or hotels if you can, and cover the keypad. And never give your card to anyone to take out money for you.
Someone would ask that?
It's rare, but it has happened to tourists. Please keep your card with you at all times.
Thank you. That's very clear.
You're welcome. Until your SIM works, the Wi-Fi password is on your key card. Please let me know if there's anything else I can do.

scenarios.title: A lost phone, the front desk and the tourist police
scenarios.setting: Front desk of a hotel inside Galle Fort, late afternoon.
scenarios.characters: Front office officer: Chandima, 28, front office officer. Tourist: Olga Ivanova, 36, from Russia, who has just come back from the lighthouse without her phone.
scenarios.resolution: Olga's phone is called and the café checked, her account is locked, and she goes to the tourist police in a ride the hotel booked, with the right details and a request for a reference number for her insurer.

notes.text: Stay calm and give one step at a time: call, check nearby, lock, report.
Do what the hotel can do for the guest (call the phone, ring the café, book the ride, print the address) instead of only giving advice.
Tell the guest what to bring before they reach the police, and mention the insurance report; stressed guests often forget it.

sayThis.say: “We need to make a police report”, not “We must put an entry at the police.”

lines.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Ivanova. You look worried. Is everything all right?
I can't find my phone. I had it at the lighthouse, and now it's gone. Maybe I left it on the wall.
I'm sorry to hear that. Let's try calling it first. May I have your number? I'll ring it from the desk phone.
Yes, here. Is it ringing?
It's ringing, but nobody's answering. Let me also call the café by the lighthouse. Sometimes people hand things in there.
Thank you. Did they find it?
I'm afraid not. Then please lock the phone from your account and change your important passwords. You're welcome to use our lobby computer.
Doing it now. What should I do next?
We should make a report with the tourist police. They help visitors with this every day, and the officers speak English.
What do I need to take?
Your passport or a copy, the hotel address, and the phone's details: the make, the colour, and the IMEI number if you have it.
The IMEI is on the box at home. My husband can send me a photo.
Perfect. Please ask the officer for a copy of the report or a reference number. Your insurance company will want it.
I didn't even think about insurance.
Many people forget. I'll book a PickMe to the police station for you, and I'll print the hotel address for the report.
Thank you. I was really panicking.
That's completely understandable. If anyone hands the phone in, we'll call you on your husband's number. The tourist hotline, 1912, can also help.
Thank you so much. You've been very kind.
It's my pleasure, Mrs. Ivanova. Your ride is outside. Please let us know how it goes.
